title: Vx: A Programming Language for Scalable, Maintainable and Secure Systems
abstract: A program for a modern machine runs on several kinds of chips. Its memory spaces, links and capacities are invisible to the compilers of today. So a host that reads device memory , a working set that does not fit, or a data race shows up only when the program runs. Vx is a systems programming language that puts these facts in the program text. A machine is a source file of declarations. A value's type says which memory it lives in. Apart from one stated exception, a function's signature is the whole contract that its callers see. A flag lists the code and the facts that the compiler trusts without a proof. This report is a tour of the language at one commit. It describes six design principles, the core language, and the features that serve three qualities. Vx is scalable because one program text runs across machines, cores and GPU threads. With an option, the compiler also checks its function bodies in parallel. It is maintainable because a signature is the contract of a function and most diagnostics have codes. The output of the parallel compiler does not depend on the number of threads. It is secure because safe code has ownership, borrow, race and placement checks, and in safe code, a file or a socket of the standard library opens only with a right. For every feature, the report gives its status and the evidence for it. It also lists where the implementation does not yet meet the design.

title: XMind: Thinking Twice via Cross-Memory Reasoning for LLM-Based Autonomous Driving
abstract: Memory-augmented large language model (LLM) driving agents can reuse past experience, yet previously learned corrections often fail to transfer when traffic conditions change. A key limitation is that existing memories mainly record observed outcomes, providing little evidence about alternative actions. We introduce XMind, a training-free framework that enables LLM-based driving to "Think Twice" through cross-memory reasoning. XMind integrates working memory of recent traffic states with episodic memory of critical risk events. The agent first makes an initial decision from the current context and then cross-checks it against retrieved historical experience. If a conflict arises, it makes a second decision guided by the retrieved evidence. To construct reliable episodic memory, XMind evaluates alternative actions through counterfactual rollouts under perturbed traffic conditions and stores the verified outcomes as structured risk capsules. These capsules are retrieved by jointly matching spatial risk patterns and scenario semantics. Across closed-loop highway simulations, XMind achieves success rates of 83.3-93.3%, exceeding the strong baseline by 6.6 percentage points on average. Evaluation on K-Risk further demonstrates lower decision risk on unseen real-world high-risk interactions. Ablation studies confirm the complementary benefits of working memory, risk-text retrieval, and counterfactual verification. Code is available at https://github.com/xiangxiangliuwo/XMind

title: OmniEVIE: Evidence-Vector-Informed Embedding for Multi-modal Retrieval
abstract: Multimodal retrieval must match dense pages, fine-grained entities, ordered video, and agent tools and memory. Single-vector embeddings lose local evidence, cross-encoders reread every recalled item online, and uncompressed late interaction is too large to serve. We present OmniEVIE, a 4.5B multi-vector embedding model covering text, images, visual documents, video, and tools with one compressed index and a three-stage retriever. Each record stores at most 128 int8 vectors of dimension 64 (9,472 bytes, or 8.82 GiB per million records), providing a mean vector, 1-bit signs, and int8 multi-vectors for coarse, middle, and final search while localizing each hit to a page region or video interval. Training, merging, indexing, and retrieval are co-designed: all tasks share one retrieval format, a three-grade evidence check removes false negatives, dynamic sampling follows the baseline-teacher gap, candidates are compressed with ST-HAC during training to match the index, stage-wise and specialist models are merged by parameter block, and a saliency gate with a noise floor refines query scoring. Trained on public datasets, OmniEVIE scores 60.68 (full d=2048 sequence) and 60.06 (K128 x d64 int8 index) on MMEB-V3 (190 tasks), 77.96 on MMEB-V2 (78 tasks), and 62.96 on ViDoRe V3 (48 tasks). On 1M and 5M records, a single-thread query takes 54.2 ms and 120.2 ms (11.1x and 25.3x faster than exact 4096-d single-vector search; 236x and 532x faster than full int8 MaxSim). Video is encoded directly from frames without a parsing model: on QVHighlights (1,083 queries), the peak falls inside the labeled segment for 78.0% of queries and the returned span (18% of video length) intersects it for 94.3% vs. 44.9% random. Weights and code: https://huggingface.co/tencent/OmniEVIE-4B and https://github.com/Tencent/OmniEVIE.

title: Transfer tensor description of driven inhomogeneous quantum systems
abstract: The transfer tensor method (TTM) extrapolates open quantum system dynamics from short-time trajectories by encoding memory effects in a discrete hierarchy of transfer tensors. Standard TTM relies on time-translational invariance (TTI) of the dynamical maps, which is broken by time-dependent driving or coherent control. We generalize TTM to time-inhomogeneous and periodically driven systems with a two-time transfer tensor hierarchy $\mathcal{T}(n,k)$. For driving with period $t_0$, sub-stroboscopic sampling ($Δt = t_0/N_c$) restores a block TTI, $\mathcal{T}(n+mN_c, k+mN_c) = \mathcal{T}(n,k)$, so that only $N_c$ starting-time branches must be learned. Averaging over the driving phase (or start time), termed temporal homogenization, restores single-index TTI at the price of phase-induced memory that combines non-additively with that of static disorder. We study two systems. (i) In an inhomogeneously broadened two-level ensemble driven beyond the rotating-wave approximation (RWA), the phase-induced memory scales with the square of the Rabi coupling and the disorder-induced memory with the square of the inhomogeneous width. The phase-induced memory is frame dependent: in the drive's rotating frame it arises solely from counter-rotating terms and vanishes under the RWA, whereas in the lab frame it largely survives the RWA. (ii) In a driven tight-binding chain at the Dunlap--Kenkre condition, the clean chain is stroboscopically frozen, whereas sub-stroboscopic tensors show that dynamical localization is enforced by delayed, period-commensurate refocusing in the memory kernel, in contrast to the immediate backflow of Anderson localization. A generalized outgoing pseudoflux tracks the non-monotonic dependence of the spreading on disorder: moderate disorder breaks the refocusing and lets the particle spread over a larger but finite region, whereas strong disorder confines it.

title: ARS-VLM: Visually Aligned Augmented Random Search for Vision-Language Models
abstract: First-order reinforcement learning, such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), is widely used to post-train Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for multimodal reasoning. However, it incurs heavy memory and system overhead from backpropagation, optimizer states, and a reference model. Forward-only zeroth-order (ZO) methods, such as Evolution Strategies (ES) and its top-k variant Augmented Random Search (ARS), avoid these overheads via reward-guided weight perturbations, yet remain unexplored for VLM reasoning. We find that directly applying standard ES or vanilla ARS to VLMs suffers from two fundamental failure modes: (i) patch-grid overfitting, fitting fragile grid-specific visual token artifacts while ignoring spatial invariants, and (ii) catastrophic forgetting, degrading general perception and out-of-distribution (OOD) tasks due to unbounded high-rank parameter and policy drift. We propose ARS-VLM, a visually aligned Augmented Random Search framework for forward-only VLM post-training. First, ARS-VLM extracts a contrastive visual basis from bilinearly paired cross-grid views, concentrating perturbations on shared visual signals while suppressing patch-shift artifacts. Second, ARS-VLM anchors shallow visual-fusion layers with a soft subspace prior while freeing deep reasoning layers, restraining policy drift without a reference model. Third, ARS-VLM scores perturbations on paired views to discard view-fragile directions during top-k selection. We evaluate ARS-VLM on Qwen3-VL-4B and Qwen3-VL-8B on multimodal reasoning tasks. On 8B, ARS-VLM reaches 61.0% validation accuracy in 20 steps versus 150 for GRPO (7.5x fewer optimization steps) and avoids the late OOD collapse of vanilla ARS and ES. Moreover, ARS-VLM achieves 75.41% single-view micro accuracy across seven OOD vision reasoning benchmarks, compared with 75.31% for full-parameter GRPO, using forward-only post-training.

title: Verifying Type Soundness for Nontransitive Information Flow Security
abstract: We present a machine-checked soundness proof of a type system for the nontransitive noninterference (NTNI) information flow security property in an imperative programming language using Dafny. The original formulation of NTNI was developed for a functional programming language augmented with memory access operators, where security policies are expressed as coarse-grained information flow constraints over component-based software systems. Although subsequent research has extended NTNI type systems in various directions, to the best of our knowledge, no prior work has established a machine-checked soundness proof for type-enforced NTNI. As a result, the correctness of existing NTNI enforcement mechanisms has not been formally verified with a high degree of assurance.

title: CoverMem: Coverage-Constrained Visual Memory for Budgeted Embodied Question Answering
abstract: Episodic-memory embodied question answering enables agents to answer questions based on previously recorded visual observations of the surrounding scenes. However, growing observation histories, varying observation quality across viewpoints, and limited computational resources make it challenging to construct and maintain compact visual memories while retrieving sufficient evidence for question answering. To address these challenges, we introduce CoverMem, which incorporates three key components: (1) a coverage-constrained memory construction method that selects a compact set of informative full frames satisfying object-quality and representative-scene coverage requirements; (2) a coverage-preserving incremental maintenance strategy that locally reselects only the affected frames to satisfy updated coverage requirements as observations arrive; and (3) a budgeted complementary frame selection method that balances question relevance, additional support for question requirements, and redundancy with selected frames within a fixed budget. Experimental results on three benchmarks covering diverse environments and question types demonstrate that CoverMem improves question-answering performance under limited visual budgets.

title: Duo: Towards Spatiotemporal Action Coordination in Bimanual Policies
abstract: Bimanual manipulation requires each arm to perform distinct motions while coordinating with the other. Common flow-based robotic policies combine both arms' actions into one token per future timestep, giving attention distinct positions across time but not across arms. We introduce Duo, a simple but effective design that models spatial and temporal dependencies within one shared action head. Specifically, Duo separates both arms into two action tokens per timestep, allowing each arm's motion to interact via cross-arm attention during flow matching. On RoboTwin 2.0, Duo improves the overall success of all four base policies, from 0.45B to 3.62B parameters, with gains of 12.55 and 9.02 percentage points for FLOWER (0.89B) and $π_{0.5}$ (3.62B), respectively. Despite its compact size, FLOWER-Duo achieves the best randomized-generalization, precision, and memory scores on RoboDojo. In real-world tasks, it outperforms $π_{0.5}$ in both success rate and execution speed, while scaling effectively with increasing training data. To provide deeper insight into the design of Duo, we conduct systematic ablations on inter-arm coordination, action grouping, and token granularity, confirming that cross-arm attention drives the improvement while arm-wise interaction offers the best accuracy-compute trade-off.

title: Rethinking Post-Training Quantization for Large Vision-Language Models
abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) compresses large vision-language models (LVLMs) by calibrating quantization parameters on a small dataset without retraining. However, despite increasingly sophisticated calibration strategies, prior methods suffer substantial performance degradation under low-bit weight--activation quantization. To understand this degradation, we locate where quantization error is concentrated and examine the corresponding weight and activation distributions. We observe that a few outliers dominate the ranges shared by per-channel (PC) weights and per-token (PT) activations, leaving insufficient resolution for most values and mapping many of them to zero. These findings motivate a shift in focus from calibration refinement to the underlying quantization representation. We therefore present Rotate-and-Refine Quantization (RRQ) as a simple, effective baseline for LVLM PTQ, combining local Hadamard transforms with group quantization and efficient group-aware execution. Across 8 multimodal tasks and diverse quantization settings, RRQ substantially outperforms baselines while reducing inference time and memory usage. At W4A4, it retains over 96\% of full-precision performance on 8B models and over 99\% on a 32B model, compared with less than 8\% for these baselines. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/kmc3661/RRQ

title: Clinical3D-Bench: Evaluating and Improving Spatial Intelligence of Multimodal LLMs in Hospital Environments
abstract: Spatial reasoning in hospitals requires tracking look-alike equipment, interpreting patient-relative directions, and judging passage widths, yet existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of these abilities. We introduce Clinical3D-Bench, a simulated benchmark with 3,368 questions of eight types on egocentric walkthroughs of 373 hospital-room layouts. Layouts follow hospital design guidelines, answers are computed from the 3D scenes, and paired scene states test whether models change their answers when relevant evidence changes. Videos are photorealistic, and ten physicians screened the layouts. Among 35 multimodal large language models (MLLMs), the best open and proprietary models reach 45.7% and 53.6% macro accuracy, against 40.8% for an answer prior and 79.0% for physicians on a subset, and 27 of 32 open models score below 40% on two-way patient-relative directions. Fine-tuning on Clinical3D-45K, our 44,750-question training set, lifts two MLLMs 16-20 points above the best proprietary model. 3D maps given to the fine-tuned MLLM as input go largely unused: replacing them with another video's, even when they are ground truth, barely changes its accuracy. The proposed GeoJeV instead lets the MLLM compute with 3D: it reconstructs a scene memory from each video, selects 3D operations and their arguments from the MLLM's question state, and adds their evidence to its option scores. It achieves the highest accuracy of all evaluated models, narrowing the gap to physicians.

title: From Memory Access to Evidence Sufficiency: Diagnosing and Addressing Demand--Evidence Misalignment
abstract: Long-term memory retrieval often returns query-relevant records, but relevance does not guarantee sufficient evidence: answering requires a set of records that jointly satisfies a question's factual, relational, temporal, and state constraints. We study this demand--evidence misalignment through MemPath, an interventional framework that diagnoses failures in memory access, demand coverage, and evidence utilization. Guided by this diagnosis, we propose BiDE-Mem, which represents questions as typed demands and uses them to guide retrieval and evidence organization. We formalize demand--evidence support; in the evaluated compact path, it is conveyed through provenance-aware evidence organization and Reader guidance rather than a separate generative four-state verification step. On LoCoMo, BiDE-Mem improves accuracy by 6.23 percentage points over Mnemis; on LongMemEval, it achieves 91.80%, with strong multi-hop and temporal performance. Supplementary Qwen-Reader evaluations place it first among seven systems on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S under two judging protocols. Ablations and evidence-level analyses show that demand representation, retrieval, and evidence presentation each contribute to answer quality.

title: KeyMemVLA: Subtask-Guided Key Memory for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation
abstract: Memory-dependent long-horizon manipulation requires vision-language-action (VLA) policies to infer task progress and recall evidence absent from current observations. Under a limited memory budget, the challenge is to retain history that resolves stage ambiguity and supports subsequent decisions. We present KeyMemVLA, a subtask-guided key memory framework based on progress indication and decision-evidence retention. A two-level annotation process selects subtasks satisfying either criterion and labels their final frames as keyframes to supervise online memory writes. A shared vision-language backbone jointly learns subtask, action, and keyframe prediction. At inference, the policy first predicts the current subtask from the instruction, visual context, and memory, then uses this semantic condition to predict actions and future memory-write positions. Actual observations are retained at the selected times during execution. We introduce KMBench to evaluate active memory retention for decisions across subtasks. Evaluations on RMBench-$M(n)$, RoboTwin-MeM, KMBench, and real-world manipulation tasks show higher average success rates than the compared baselines. Ablation studies and representation analysis support the roles of key memory and explicit task-progress semantics. These results highlight the value of coupling sparse key memory with online progress inference for history-dependent control.

title: Synchronized Memory -Dependent Intracellular Oscillations for a Cell-Bulk ODE-PDE Model in $\mathbb{R}^3$
abstract: We develop a hybrid asymptotic-numerical theory for a cell-bulk ODE-PDE model in $\mathbb{R}^3$ to analyze the long-range diffusive coupling of spatially localized, dynamically active cells. In the limit of small cell radius $\varepsilon\ll 1$, we derive a novel integro-differential ODE system for the intracellular dynamics, in which the 3-D bulk diffusion field is effectively replaced by a time- memory kernel whose strength depends on the inter-cell distances. To compute long-time solutions efficiently, we implement a fast time-marching scheme for this integro-differential system that is inspired by the \emph{sum-of-exponentials} method. This scheme is applied to Sel'kov intracellular kinetics, which is a conceptual two-component model for a conditional oscillator. Our analysis reveals that, in contrast to the more strongly coupled 2-D case, each cell in $\mathbb{R}^3$ experiences only a weak $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon)$ coupling effect from the other cells in the population. Consequently, individual cells that exhibit oscillatory intracellular dynamics can only synchronize over very long time scales of order $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-1})$ when they are separated by $\mathcal{O}(1)$ distances. Moreover, cells whose kinetic parameters are $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon)$ close to their marginal stability threshold will be influenced by the weak $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon)$ cell-cell coupling from the entire population. In order to resolve the effect of these subtle interactions on collective intracellular dynamics, we develop a novel matrix perturbation theory for the linear stability of steady-state solutions of the cell-bulk model. Finally, we validate our analytical predictions of the perturbed marginal stability thresholds of steady-state solutions using the time-marching numerical scheme, illustrating various types of synchronized intracellular dynamics that can emerge over long time scales.

title: Efficient Semantic ORDER BY via Transitivity-Aware LLM Batch Sorting
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) enable declarative semantic sorting through LLM-ORDER BY operators that rank tuples according to natural-language criteria over unstructured data. Executing such operators efficiently is challenging because LLM comparisons are expensive, stochastic, and sometimes inconsistent. Pairwise approaches require many costly calls. Listwise approaches such as external merge sort rank several items per call, but they follow a fixed merge schedule and keep no record of earlier answers: each merge call re-asks orderings that previous calls have already revealed, directly or by transitivity. We present Transitive Batched Sort (TBS), a transitivity-aware physical operator for semantic sorting that records every revealed preference in a global acyclic preference graph and issues a listwise request only for items whose relative order is not yet implied. To scale, TBS stores only directly observed preferences and answers transitivity queries through a memory -efficient reachability index; to handle noisy LLM outputs, it validates responses and rejects cycle-inducing updates. We evaluate TBS on six benchmarks spanning structured sorting, product price ranking, passage ranking, and personalized recommendation with four LLMs. TBS reduces API calls by 12-20x relative to pairwise quicksort and, at the same batch size, uses 1.1-1.6x fewer calls and 1.3-5.3x lower cost than listwise merge sort while achieving competitive or higher ranking quality across most benchmarks; on Amazon it scales to one million products. These results show that reusing previously inferred preference relations, rather than re-querying them, is an effective foundation for scalable semantic ORDER BY operators.

title: Integral DeltaNet: Improved Linear Attention with Adaptive Memory Integration
abstract: Linear attention replaces softmax attention with a linear formulation, enabling linear-time computation with a fixed-size recurrent state instead of a growing key-value cache. These computational and memory advantages have attracted growing interest in linear attention for long-context language modeling. However, compressing past information into a fixed-size state causes memory collisions that hinder long-context understanding. Although DeltaNet mitigates memory collisions through delta-rule updates and Gated DeltaNet extends this approach with gating, these mechanisms may also discard information relevant to future predictions. To address this limitation, we introduce Integral DeltaNet, which maintains two complementary recurrent states: a fast-updating delta state that captures current key-value associations and an integral state that preserves a weighted history of the delta state. At readout, the model adaptively combines these states to access information across different timescales. We further derive a chunkwise parallel formulation that enables hardware-efficient training. We evaluate Integral DeltaNet using 340M and 1.3B parameter models trained from scratch on 15B and 100B FineWeb-Edu tokens, respectively. Comparisons with strong recurrent baselines show improved overall performance in language modeling, commonsense reasoning, real-world and synthetic retrieval, long-context understanding, and length extrapolation. We also compare training throughput and activation memory, as well as decoding latency and memory.

title: Generalized Tensor Parallelism: Powering Trillion-Parameter LLM Training at 10+ EFLOP/s
abstract: Pretraining state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs) with up to trillions of parameters is memory - and compute-intensive. Existing parallelization schemes compromise on either per-GPU memory or throughput: data parallelism replicates parameters; tensor parallelism and fully sharded data parallelism (FSDP) add communication of activations and parameters, respectively, to every microbatch; and pipeline parallelism leaves GPUs idle while the pipeline fills and drains. We show that, for linear layers, five commonly used parallelisms (data, tensor, sequence, context parallelism and FSDP) are special cases of one framework, generalized tensor parallelism (GTP), in which each layer's parameters and activations are partitioned and either can be re-materialized with an all-gather before use. In GTP, a parameter all-gather is an optional preprocessing step on one input of a matrix multiplication (GEMM), whereas FSDP implementations typically treat it as a step before an entire Transformer block, which can increase memory footprint and delay GEMMs. The GTP view lets us schedule all-gathers per GEMM rather than per block, issuing each early enough to hide its communication but late enough to limit memory . Our implementation is open source at https://github.com/NVIDIA/Megatron-LM; with it, an internal 2T-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model reaches \textbf{13.0 model EFLOP/s} (exaFLOP/s) on 12,288 GB300 GPUs with 98\% weak-scaling efficiency, and runs with 1M-token sequences on 512 GPUs. On 256--1,024 GPUs, our implementation achieves \textbf{1.05--1.55$\times$ the throughput of Megatron-FSDP} across three MoE models and \textbf{1.27--1.31$\times$ that of a tuned 3D-parallel recipe with pipeline parallelism} on a DeepSeek-V4-Pro proxy model.

title: RoboHarness-RL: Agentic Reinforcement Learning for VLM-Based Robot Manipulation
abstract: Agentic harnesses enable frontier vision-language models (VLMs) to manipulate robots through perception, planning, and control tools, yet achieving comparable performance with compact open-weight VLMs remains challenging. We present RoboHarness-RL, an agentic reinforcement learning framework for improving VLM-based robot manipulation through tool calls. Starting from supervised fine-tuning on successful teacher demonstrations, the VLM further improves through multi-turn reinforcement learning with task-outcome rewards, without relying on vision-language-action models or world action models. To support efficient multi-turn training, we develop LiteHarness, which uses hierarchical memory to keep interaction contexts compact while preserving task performance. With Qwen3.5-9B, RL raises success from 31.2% to 44.0% on RoboTwin 2.0 and from 57.8% to 73.3% on LIBERO-Pro; these gains extend to randomized RoboTwin scenes unseen during training (26.4% to 38.0%). Behavioral analysis further shows that RL reduces repetitive-call rates by up to $4\times$, shortens successful executions, and improves recovery from negative feedback. Project page: https://aim-uofa.github.io/RoboHarness-RL/
